<reason>Both sides were strong, but B won the decisive clashes. A's risky claim that hospital coverage via "more shifts staffed by more people" was "the mechanism working" became a concession B exploited relentlessly: it admitted a pure cost increase with zero productivity offset in continuous-coverage sectors. A's honest answer to B's best pressure question ("the public purse pays it") let B frame the mandate as a massive spending program smuggled through labor law — "a statute is not a funding source" — which A's burnout-budget reframe never quantitatively answered. B also fielded A's pressure questions well: the incidence distinction (forty answered near-universal harm with economy-wide gains; thirty-two imposes costs on all for sectoral gains) defused the repeal-the-weekend trap, and B actually named a counter-policy (a 32-hour overtime threshold without pay protection) that escapes the first-mover trap, blunting A's coordination argument. A's strongest surviving material — net-vs-gross costs, the Ford precedent, "uncosted-to-the-firm is not costless to society" — kept the debate close, and A's closing attack on B's alternative was partially blunted by B's point that premium pricing raises pay for retained hours. B's consistent weighing (certain/universal costs vs. sectoral/conditional benefits) gave the cleaner reason to vote. Both sides had clipped turns as execution costs; both used proper Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: asked directly who pays in hospitals, B transformed A's "the public purse pays it" concession into the debate's centerpiece — an enormous spending program routed through labor law to avoid a budget debate — and then reversed A's own Ford precedent ("statute is needed exactly where the math fails, which is precisely where the mandate inflicts pure loss").</best_rebuttal>
